facts.claim: American Man was released October 30, 2015 on Bloodshot Records and was The Yawpers' first release for the label.
The album was produced by Cracker guitarist and co-founder Johnny Hickman. Discogs credits production to Hickman and The Yawpers, and credits The Yawpers with writing.

Discogs credits Nate Cook with vocals and guitar and Noah Shomberg with drums and vocals. It credits Andrew Berlin as recording engineer, Bill Douglass with additional recording, and Jim Wilson with mastering.
The album was recorded at the Blasting Room, the Colorado studio owned by Descendents drummer Bill Stevenson.
The album was recorded live to tape over a four-day session. Most of the material was written by Nate Cook in a 'feverish' stretch in February and March 2014.

Nate Cook said the title track is written from the perspective of someone from his conservative small-town Texas hometown, someone so nationalistic they lose touch with reality, which he called 'Patriotism to the point of psychosis.'

Cook said the title track is written from the perspective of someone he doesn't necessarily agree with. He said the album is written from the perspectives of characters who don't always share his views.

American Man is a 12-song set loosely based on the American West, told through 12 different narrators. Cook said it began as a concept record in which he wrote each song from a different American character's perspective.
Bloodshot signed the band after a SXSW 2015 showcase in Austin. The label offered a three-record deal for an album the band had finished in 2014.

The Yawpers formed in 2011 around frontman Nate Cook and lead guitarist Jesse Parmet, and self-released their debut album Capon Crusade in 2012. The follow-up Bloodshot album, Boy in a Well, came out in October 2017.

research.lineage: The Yawpers sit in the Colorado and Bloodshot Records tradition of punk-inflected roots rock, blending blues and country with punk energy and Walt Whitman-inspired lyrics.

draft:
The scariest line in **American Man** is a prayer: "I pray to God that I never have to take it too far." The narrator sings it in the chorus, twice, and means it each time. He doesn't want to hurt anyone. He also has guns, a grievance, and a flag, and the song spends four and a half minutes watching those things pull against his hope.

Nate Cook wrote it from inside the head of someone from his conservative small-town Texas hometown, a man he called a case of "patriotism to the point of psychosis." Cook has said he doesn't necessarily agree with him. The song never sneers, though. It's one of twelve narrators on The Yawpers' Bloodshot debut, a loose concept record about the American West, and Cook gives this one real grief to carry. The man's father held the ground sacred. Now the streets are trash, the culture wars are lost, and "This is my home and I'm a stranger here." That's displacement, the ache of outliving the world you were raised for, and it sits right next to the self-pity and the menace without canceling them out. He's too dried up to cry, he says, and in the next verse he's bringing the plague.

The music refuses to panic with him. A clean electric guitar rolls through arpeggiated chords, the bass walks underneath, and the drums keep a plain, unhurried beat at a moderate pace. Cook sings in a slightly raspy, conversational mid-range with no harmonies to soften it. It's dry and close, recorded live to tape over four days at the Blasting Room, Bill Stevenson's Colorado studio, with Cracker's Johnny Hickman producing. The raw, small-room sound makes the narrator feel like he's talking across a kitchen table, calm enough that you almost nod along.

That's the trick of it. Bloodshot's punk-inflected roots rock usually burns hot. Here the heat stays in the words. The flag goes from grand to hollow, its applause canned. He salutes her with blood on his hands. Then the last chorus turns the violence inward: "I'll die for her and by my own hand." The devotion and the despair end up the same act, and the band chants the title over and over until the lyric marks it to fade.

You come out of it understanding a man you'd cross the street to avoid, which is harder and more useful than hating him.
